'''Ann C. Noble''' is a [[Sensory analysis|sensory]] [[chemist]] and retired professor from the [[University of California, Davis]]. During her time at the [[UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology]], Noble and her colleagues developed the "Wine Aroma Wheel"<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Noble |first1=A. C. |last2=Arnold |first2=R. A. |last3=Masuda |first3=B. M. |last4=Pecore |first4=S. D. |last5=Schmidt |first5=J. O. |last6=Stern |first6=P. M. |title=Progress Towards a Standardized System of Wine Aroma Terminology |journal=American Journal of Enology and Viticulture |date=1984 |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=107–109 |doi=10.5344/ajev.1984.35.2.107 |url=https://www.ajevonline.org/content/35/2/107 |access-date=13 February 2026|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which has enhanced the public understanding of [[wine tasting]] and [[List of wine tasting descriptors|terminology]].<ref name="Oxford pg 35-36">J. Robinson (ed) ''"The Oxford Companion to Wine"'' Third Edition pg 35-36 Oxford University Press 2006 {{ISBN|978-0-19-860990-2}}</ref> At the time of her hiring at UC Davis in 1974, Noble was the first woman hired as a faculty member of the Viticulture department.<ref name="Alley">L. Alley ''"[https://web.archive.org/web/20040224135323/http://www.winespectator.com/Wine/Daily/News/0%2C1145%2C1804%2C00.html Wine Sensory Scientist Ann Noble Retires From UC Davis]"'' [[Wine Spectator]], August 21, 2002.</ref> Noble retired from Davis in 2002 and in 2003 was named [[Emeritus]] Professor of [[Enology]]. Since retirement she has participated as a judge in the [[San Francisco Chronicle]] [[Wine Competition]].<ref name="San Fran">San Francisco Chronicle ''"[http://www.winejudging.com/bios/ann_noble.htm Ann Noble bio]"'' Wine Judge: Accessed Dec. 16th, 2007  {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101204042755/http://winejudging.com/bios/ann_noble.htm |date=4 December 2010 }}</ref>

==Career==
After earning her [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in [[Food science]] from the [[University of Massachusetts Amherst]], Noble was hired by UC Davis in 1974 to work in their sensory research program.<ref name="Alley"/> After studying the techniques and application of [[wine]] tasting, Noble discovered that there was no objective framework or widely agreed upon terminology that a wine taster could use to describe things such as "earthy" [[aroma (wine)|aromas]] or the different smells of various [[fruit]]s that can show up in a wine. In 1984, her research lead her to develop the "Aroma Wheel".<ref name="Oxford pg 35-36"/> Other research work went into how a wine's aroma and flavor can influence [[consumer]] choices as well as how wine tasters perceive [[astringency]] in wine.<ref name="Alley"/> Noble, in addition to her work on the wine aroma wheel, also did research on multivariate statistics of sensory data and its applications. She also published over 150 research papers in her time there.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.congress.gov/congressional-record/2013/12/5/extensions-of-remarks-section/article/E1794-3|title=Congressional Record|website=www.congress.gov|access-date=2016-04-05}}</ref>

===The Aroma Wheel===
The Aroma Wheel provides a visual graphic of the different categories and aroma components that one can encounter in wine. The terminology used is standardized for use by both professionals and amateur wine tasters. Aroma is identified by the olfactory bulb from through inhalation of the wine's scent, and is used to identify the flavors from the grape itself. Bouquet refers to compounds that can affect the flavours, such as sugar, oak, and acid.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://winingways.wordpress.com/2011/05/16/wine-aroma-wheel/|title=Wine Aroma Wheel|last=WiningWays|website=WiningWays|access-date=2016-04-05|date=2011-05-16}}</ref> The aroma wheel does not contain terms to describe texture or [[mouthfeel]], however these are listed in the Australian "Mouthfeel Wheel". A separate Aroma Wheel has also been created for [[sparkling wine]]. The wheel breaks down wine aromas into 12 basic categories and then further sub-divided into different aromas that can fall into those main categories.<ref name="Oxford pg 35-36"/>
* [[Chemical]] – Includes aromas like [[sulfur]] and [[petroleum]]
* [[Pungent]] – Aromas like [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]
* [[Oxidized]] – Aromas like [[acetaldehyde]]
* [[Microbiological]] – Aromas like [[yeast (wine)|yeast]] and [[lactic acid]]
* [[Floral]] – Aromas like ''[[Pelargonium]]'' geraniums and [[linalool]]
* [[Spicy]] – Aromas like [[licorice]] and [[anise]]
* [[Fruity]] – Aromas like [[blackcurrant]] and [[apricot]]
* [[Vegetation|Vegetative]] – Aromas like [[eucalyptus]] and [[artichoke]]
* [[Nut (fruit)|Nutty]] – Aromas like [[walnut]] and [[hazelnut]]
* [[Caramelized]] – Aromas like [[butterscotch]] and [[molasses]]
* [[Wood]]y – Aromas often imparted by [[oak (wine)|oak]] like [[vanilla]] and [[coffee]]
* Earthy – Aromas such as [[mushroom]] and [[mildew]]

The [[German Wine Institute]] has created a special [[German language]] version of the Aroma Wheel meant to be specially adapted to [[German wine]]s, with one wheel for white wines and one wheel for red wines.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.deutscheweine.de/internet-de/nav/74c/74c492b8-e441-6117-3d28-952196117f51$08b709dd-d602-3401-be59-267b48205846.htm |title=Deutscheweine.de: Das Wein-Aromarad |access-date=30 December 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080304180152/http://www.deutscheweine.de/internet-de/nav/74c/74c492b8-e441-6117-3d28-952196117f51$08b709dd-d602-3401-be59-267b48205846.htm |archive-date=4 March 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, in the translation they removed the petroleum smell (and the entire "chemical" category) from the white wine wheel, despite the fact that mature [[Riesling]] wines - Germany's signature grape variety - are the best-known examples of wines that show this aroma. It seems that the motive for omitting the reference to petroleum was that many consumers perceive it as a "negative" aroma. The Institute's move has been criticized by foreign experts on German wines.<ref name="O. Bird petrol">Owen Bird, ''Rheingold - The German Wine Renaissance'', Arima Publishing 2005, pp. 90-97 {{ISBN|978-1-84549-079-9}}</ref>

== Post-retirement ==
Noble currently teaches classes domestically and internationally. She also continues to work as a wine judge. She participates in meetings concerning Wine, Science, and Sensometrics in the U.S. and overseas. She is also writing a book on Wine Sensory evaluation.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://wineserver.ucdavis.edu/people/emeriti/noble.html|title=Ann C. Noble {{!}} Viticulture & Enology|website=wineserver.ucdavis.edu|access-date=2016-04-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160505164722/http://wineserver.ucdavis.edu/people/emeriti/noble.html|archive-date=2016-05-05|url-status=dead}}</ref>

* 1994 – Honorary Research Lecturer, American Society of Viticulture and Enology<ref name="San Fran" />
* 2000 – Award of Merit, [[American Wine Society]]<ref name="San Fran" />
* 2001 – Outstanding women in [[California wine]] industry award, ''[[Decanter Magazine]]''<ref name="San Fran"/>
* 2012 – One of “The 50 Most Powerful Women in Wine",  ''The Drinks Business''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thedrinksbusiness.com/2012/12/top-50-most-powerful-women-in-wine-50-41/7/|title=Top 50 most powerful women in wine: 50 – 41|website=www.thedrinksbusiness.com|date=5 December 2012 |access-date=2016-04-05}}</ref>
